items.title: Some northeast districts have their own migration corridors for jobs in southern India, reveals survey

Guwahati-headquartered Seven Sisters Development Assistance, a non-profit organisation, conducted the survey covering 693 households across five districts in Assam, two in Meghalaya and one in Tripura.
About 62% of these households belong to Scheduled Tribe communities and 95% own land but not enough to farm.
Some 88% of those surveyed cite a lack of work in the village, while 91% name at least one “push” factor, such as shortage of land or the need to repay loans.
According to the survey, 72.6% of the migrants work outside their home State following “well-worn corridors”.
Karnataka tops the chart with 22.7% of the outflow, followed by Assam (mainly Guwahati) with 22.3%, Tamil Nadu with 13.8% and Kerala with 10.1%.

items.title: Shipping Emissions Cost The Global Economy $963 Billion Between 1990 To 2020, New Study Finds
points: A new study by Zero Carbon Analytics finds that emissions from international shipping cost the global economy around USD 963 billion between 1990 and 2020.
These economic impacts are projected to worsen with continued emissions growth if business-as-usual continues, and could outweigh the cost of action to reduce emissions in the sector.

The findings come as governments at the UN’s International Maritime Organization (IMO) resume talks on 23 November on adopting the Net-Zero Framework (NZF), a climate policy to cut emissions from ships.
The study finds that international shipping’s share of global emissions has caused the US USD 280.7 billion in damages, China USD 113.5 billion, and Japan USD 66.8 billion.
Damages attributable to international shipping emissions reduced the United Arab Emirates’ 2020 GDP by 0.35%, Saudi Arabia’s by 0.34%, Mali’s by 0.32%, and Burkina Faso’s by 0.3%.
Implementing and acting on the NZF could avoid approximately 14.2 billion tonnes of CO2-equivalent emissions between 2026 and 2050, compared to business-as-usual.

items.title: EU court hands Russian Maritime Register partial sanctions victory
points: Russia’s state-owned ship classification society has secured a partial legal victory against European Union sanctions, with judges overturning a decision to permanently withdraw its recognition while upholding the majority of restrictions against it.

The EU’s General Court ruled yesterday that the withdrawal of recognition from the Russian Maritime Register of Shipping (RMRS) was disproportionate because suspending its approval would have achieved the same objective.
The St. Petersburg-headquartered organisation, which has held EU recognition since 1998, was targeted following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Brussels imposed investment and transaction bans, withdrew the society’s authorisation to inspect and certify EU-flagged vessels and prohibited ships certified by RMRS from entering European ports and locks.

Judges found that permanently removing recognition went too far because the organisation would have to undergo an entirely new approval process if sanctions were subsequently lifted, with no guarantee of success.
However, the court rejected most of RMRS’s challenge, including its objections to financial restrictions.
The ruling does not immediately restore the society’s European operating rights.
